query: Which material can be used for lightweight and superior comprehensive performance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy alloy designed with a significant fraction of a lightweight element (titanium) in a CoCrFeNiTi composition will exhibit a lower overall density and a favorable balance of mechanical properties (strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance) compared to similar traditional HEAs lacking titanium.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, as-cast or heat-treated CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy, prepared to form a stable solid solution.
generation.intervention: Incorporate titanium into the equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy formulation to replace part of heavier elements.
generation.conditions: Performance to be evaluated at room temperature and at moderately elevated temperatures (below ~750 °C) where the single-phase structure remains stable.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a single-phase solid solution with substantial lattice distortion due to the multi-principal element design, where titanium contributes to reduced density.
generation.mechanism: The high entropy effect and lattice distortion promote a unique deformation behavior (such as deformation twinning and transformation-induced plasticity) that, together with titanium’s lower atomic mass, reduce density while retaining mechanical integrity and resistance to corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The CoCrFeNiTi alloy is expected to demonstrate a lower density and comparable or improved strength–ductility balance relative to traditional heavy HEAs, leading to superior comprehensive performance in structural applications under the specified conditions.
generation.baseline: The performance characteristics (density, strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance) of conventional HEAs with similar principal elements but without the targeted titanium addition.
generation.boundary: At temperatures above ~750 °C, potential phase decomposition (e.g., formation of brittle sigma or BCC phases) may occur, limiting the benefits of the lightweight design in high-temperature applications.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in density reduction and mechanical performance are not precisely known, and the extent to which titanium addition may influence long-term phase stability and degradation under cyclic thermal loading remains to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA samples: one with a CoCrFeNiTi composition and one with a similar heavy-element based HEA lacking significant titanium content. Subject both samples to identical processing and heat-treatment procedures and then test them under controlled laboratory conditions.
measurements: Assess phase composition and structural stability via X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy.
Measure mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility) over a range of temperatures (room temperature to 750 °C).
Evaluate corrosion resistance in relevant oxidative or molten salt environments.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CoCrFeNiTi alloy does not exhibit significantly lower density (within measurement resolution) and fails to demonstrate a comparable or improved strength–ductility balance relative to the heavy-element HEA under the defined temperature range, or if undesirable phase transformations occur well below 750 °C, then the hypothesis is falsified.

4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.

The appearance of high entropy alloys breaks the traditional design concept of alloys based on mixing enthalpy and opens up a broad space for composition design for the research and development of new materials. The comprehensive effect of the mixing of various main elements endows the high entropy alloy with high entropy effect in thermodynamics, lattice distortion effect in structure, hysteresis diffusion effect in dynamics, and “cocktail” effect in performance [ [1] , [2] ]. The principle of multi-principal element design based on these four effects results in the high entropy alloy showing many unique properties beyond the traditional alloy. These characteristics cover excellent corrosion resistance [ [3] ], wear resistance [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ], excellent fatigue strength, and yield strength under various temperature conditions [ [10] , [11] ], high hardness [ [12] ], excellent microstructure stability and thermal stability [ [13] , [14] ], and excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [15] ]. High–entropy alloys (HEAs) have had remarkable progress and advancement since their development by Professor Yeh in 2004. The term “high–entropy alloy” generally refers to a single–phase solid solution alloy with a simple crystal structure composed of five or more elements, with an atomic percentage ranging from 5% to 35% [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. Given their superior hardness, exceptional strength, resistance to corrosion, and a multitude of additional benefits, HEAs have became a new type of alloy material that has received a great deal of attention in the research field during recent years and the hot point of many researches [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. The high–entropy alloy composed of five elements–Cobalt (Co), Chromium (Cr), Iron (Fe), Nickel (Ni), and Titanium (Ti)–in equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions exhibited a simple solid solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability. However, it suffered from a relatively low hardness and strength [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. The existing research lacked a comprehensive and thorough understanding of the microstructure and deformation dynamics of the CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy.
